query: What additive manufacturing strategy and post-processing route can enable the fabrication of a refractory high-entropy alloy family (Group IV-V transition metals) capable of retaining high-temperature structural integrity, and what specific microstructural state is hypothesized to optimize mechanical performance while mitigating the inherent brittleness associated with interstitial impurities?

generation.target_system: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy (RHEA) family based on Group IV-V transition metals (Nb, Ta, Mo, W, V), processed via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) with a post-processing route involving stepwise coherent nanoprecipitation (SCCP) heat treatment. The target microstructure is an 'inverted' BCC matrix with discrete, coherent B2 (ordered) nanoprecipitates.

generation.hypothesis: Fabrication of a Group IV-V refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 or NbMoTaW) via Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using mixed elemental powders will produce a metastable single-phase BCC solid solution with a cellular/dendritic microstructure. Subsequent post-processing via a multi-step heat treatment (aging) will induce the formation of Stepwise Controllable Coherent Nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) of an ordered B2 phase within the disordered BCC matrix. This creates an 'inverted' microstructure where discrete, coherent B2 precipitates are dispersed in a continuous BCC matrix. This specific state is hypothesized to optimize mechanical performance by enabling dislocation shearing of the coherent precipitates (similar to Ni-superalloys) while maintaining the ductility of the BCC matrix, thereby mitigating the inherent brittleness caused by interstitial impurities and the continuous ordered phase found in as-cast or as-built states.
generation.material_initial_state: Mixed elemental powders of Group IV-V transition metals (W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V) with equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, processed via LPBF to form a dense, single-phase BCC solid solution with a fine cellular/dendritic microstructure.
generation.intervention: Post-build heat treatment consisting of a solution annealing step followed by a stepwise aging protocol designed to nucleate and grow coherent B2 nanoprecipitates (SCCPs) without coarsening or losing coherency.
generation.conditions: Additive manufacturing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) with linear energy density optimized for full fusion (e.g., >2.5 J/mm). Post-processing: Aging temperatures between 600°C and 900°C, with specific dwell times to control precipitate size (nanoscale, <10-20 nm) and volume fraction.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent B2 (ordered) nanoprecipitates embedded in a disordered BCC matrix. The coherent interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion that are overcome by shearing, facilitating dislocation transmission and relieving stress concentrations.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is derived from the transfer of the 'Stepwise Controllable Coherent Nanoprecipitations' (SCCP) concept from PMC10213035 and the 'inverted microstructure' concept from PMC5995863. The coherent B2 precipitates impede dislocation motion to increase strength (Orowan or shearing mechanism), but unlike continuous ordered phases, the discrete nature and coherency allow dislocations to transmit across interfaces, preventing premature crack initiation and maintaining ductility. This mitigates the brittleness typically associated with interstitial impurities in BCC refractory alloys by providing a more uniform stress distribution and preventing the formation of brittle continuous networks.
generation.predicted_outcome: The optimized alloy will exhibit an ultrahigh yield strength (>1.0 GPa at 800°C) and tensile ductility (>10-15% at ambient temperature), significantly outperforming the as-built single-phase state which typically suffers from low ductility. The material will retain structural integrity at elevated temperatures (up to 800-900°C) due to the thermal stability of the coherent B2 precipitates.
generation.baseline: As-built LPBF RHEAs typically exhibit a single-phase BCC structure with high strength but poor ductility (<5%) due to the continuous ordered phase or segregation of brittle phases, and high hardness but limited toughness.
generation.boundary: The strategy is applicable to BCC-structured Group IV-V RHEAs. It may not transfer to FCC-based RHEAs or systems where the B2 phase is incoherent or forms a continuous network. The heat treatment window is narrow; excessive aging will lead to precipitate coarsening and loss of coherency, reverting to a brittle state.
generation.uncertainty: The exact heat treatment parameters (temperature/time) required to achieve the optimal 'inverted' microstructure for specific compositions (e.g., W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 vs. NbMoTaW) are uncertain and will require empirical optimization. The stability of the coherent precipitates under prolonged high-temperature service (>1000 hours) is also uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via LPBF. Apply a standard aging heat treatment intended to form B2 precipitates. Perform TEM to verify the presence of coherent B2 precipitates and tensile testing at room temperature and 800°C.
measurements: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) for precipitate size, spacing, and coherency
Tensile testing (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation) at RT and 800°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if: (1) TEM shows no formation of coherent B2 precipitates after the heat treatment, or (2) the resulting material exhibits brittle fracture (ductility < 5%) despite the presence of precipitates, indicating the 'inverted' microstructure failed to relieve stress concentrations or the precipitates are incoherent/continuous.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

High entropy or multi principal element alloys are a promising and relatively young concept for designing alloys. The idea of creating alloys without a single main alloying element opens up a wide space for possible new alloy compositions. High entropy alloys based on refractory metals such as W, Mo, Ta or Nb are of interest for future high temperature applications e.g., in the aerospace or chemical industry. However, producing refractory metal high entropy alloys by conventional metallurgical methods remains challenging. For this reason, the feasibility of laser-based additive manufacturing of the refractory metal high entropy alloy W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 by laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) is investigated in the present work. In-situ alloy formation from mixtures of easily available elemental powders is employed to avoid an expensive atomization of pre-alloyed powder. It is shown that PBF-LB/M of W 20 Mo 20 Ta 20 Nb 20 V 20 is in general possible and that a complete fusion of the powder mixture without a significant number of undissolved particles is achievable by in-situ alloy formation during PBF-LB/M when selecting favorable process parameter combinations.
